text: Parsing the SMILES: CC1=C(C(=O)OCc2ccccc2)C(c2ccccc2)NC(=O)N1C. The core is a six-membered dihydropyrimidinone ring containing two nitrogens, one of which is N-methylated, with a cyclic urea carbonyl. The ring carries a methyl group and a benzyl ester on the alkene carbons, and a phenyl group sits on the sp3 carbon between the alkene and the NH. Two monocyclic benzene rings are present as pendant aryl groups, with no ring fusion. The molecule has one NH hydrogen-bond donor and several acceptors from the carbonyl oxygens. The ring is partly rigid due to the alkene and urea, while the benzyl ester adds rotational flexibility. There is no molecular symmetry, since the substituents are distinct.

This molecule is built from two pyrazolone rings joined by a methylene bridge at their 4-positions. Each pyrazolone is a five-membered ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms and a carbonyl group, with a methyl group on the ring carbon and an N-phenyl group on one nitrogen, while the other nitrogen carries a methyl group. The two ring units are chemically identical, so the overall structure has an approximate two-fold symmetry about the central CH2 linker. Each pyrazolone carbonyl acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are substituted. The two phenyl rings add bulk and aromatic character, and the connecting methylene bridge gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzoic acid derivative, meaning a single benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group directly attached to the ring. The benzene core is a flat, fully aromatic six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid, with only the carboxylic acid group able to rotate about its single bond to the ring. Two halogen substituents sit on the ring: a bromine atom ortho to the carboxylic acid and a fluorine atom para to it, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the halogens are weak acceptors only.

This molecule is a 1,4-benzodioxane scaffold, meaning a benzene ring fused to a six-membered 1,4-dioxane ring through two adjacent aromatic carbons bearing ether oxygens. The saturated dioxane ring carries a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) on the carbon next to one ring oxygen, so the stereocenter at that position makes the substitution pattern asymmetric. The benzo portion is unsubstituted, and the bicyclic framework is largely rigid while the dioxane ring can adopt a half-chair conformation. The two ring ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the primary alcohol provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site.

The molecule is built around a five-membered isoxazolone-type ring, containing an oxygen and a nitrogen atom adjacent to each other, with a carbonyl group on the ring carbon next to the oxygen. A methyl group is attached to the ring carbon that is double-bonded to nitrogen. The ring's other carbon bears an exocyclic hydrazone-like linkage, C=N-NH, which connects to a phenyl ring. That phenyl ring carries a chlorine atom on the position adjacent to the point of attachment, giving an ortho-substitution pattern. The conjugated system is largely planar, which gives the molecule considerable rigidity, with only the single bonds to the methyl group and the chlorophenyl unit permitting rotation. The N-H donor and the carbonyl and ring oxygen and nitrogen acceptors give it hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a secosteroid built on a fused polycyclic scaffold with a conjugated triene linking two ring systems. One ring system is a hydrindane-type bicyclic core bearing an angular methyl group and a branched eight-carbon side chain ending in an isopropyl terminus, which is flexible. The other ring is a cyclohexane-type ring carrying an exocyclic methylene group and two secondary hydroxyl substituents at positions 1 and 3, giving it hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability. The molecule has no symmetry, and its diene and triene segments impart partial rigidity while the saturated side chain and ring CH2 units remain flexible.

text: The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic core in which a pyridine ring is fused to a coumarin-type lactone ring and a benzene ring, giving a largely planar, rigid aromatic framework. A 2-ethylamino substituent (an N-ethyl amine attached to the carbon next to the pyridine nitrogen) sits on the pyridine ring, while an ethyl ester group (an ethoxycarbonyl) is attached at the adjacent carbon. The lactone carbonyl and ester carbonyl oxygens, together with the pyridine nitrogen, act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the secondary amine N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The structure lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents occupy non-equivalent positions, and only the terminal ethyl groups show some conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three tert-butyl groups, each a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, are attached at alternating positions around the ring, and a primary amino group sits on the carbon between two of them. The arrangement gives the ring a 2,4,6-trisubstituted pattern, with the amine flanked on both sides by bulky tert-butyl groups. The tert-butyl groups are large, rigid, and nonpolar, so the molecule is conformationally restricted and is not symmetric about all axes because the amine breaks the threefold pattern. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the rest of the molecule offers no hydrogen-bonding sites.

The molecule is a semicarbazone built around a linear chain carrying a phenyl ring. A benzene ring sits at one end, attached through a three-carbon chain to a carbon that is double-bonded to a nitrogen, forming a C=N hydrazone-type linkage. That nitrogen connects to a urea-like unit, a carbonyl flanked by an NH and a terminal NH2 group. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so it has no substitution pattern to speak of, and the molecule has no stereocenters and no element of symmetry beyond the planar phenyl ring. The chain and the N–N–C linkage give it considerable conformational flexibility, with only the aromatic ring and the C=N bond being rigid. The NH and NH2 groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and imine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a flavonol-type scaffold built from a fused benzopyranone (chromone) core, with a phenyl ring attached at the 2-position of the pyranone ring. The bicyclic chromone system is planar and fully aromatic-like, which makes the overall framework rigid, with the 2-phenyl ring able to rotate only slightly about its single bond to the core. Two hydroxyl groups are present: one on the 3-position of the pyranone ring and one on the benzo ring at the 7-position, while the ring carbonyl at the 4-position acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the two hydroxyls sit on different rings and the pendant phenyl is unsubstituted. Together, the hydroxyl groups and carbonyl oxygen give it multiple hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

This molecule is a branched, fully saturated-except-for-one-site aliphatic hydrocarbon built on a linear chain of nine carbons. Its backbone is an open chain with no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms. The one unsaturation is a terminal carbon-carbon double bond, with a methyl group on the internal alkene carbon, which creates a short branch at one end of the chain. Because the molecule lacks any symmetry-breaking polar groups beyond the alkene, its structure is essentially nonpolar, and it is highly flexible due to free rotation about its single bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a single methylene (CH2) bridge, giving a diarylmethane scaffold with no fused ring systems. Each phenyl ring carries one fluorine atom located para to the bridging carbon, so the substitution pattern is symmetric, and the molecule as a whole possesses approximately twofold symmetry through the central CH2 group. The aromatic rings are planar and rigid, while the methylene linker allows rotation about its two C–C bonds, giving the molecule moderate conformational flexibility. The structure contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, and the fluorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring linked through a single methylene (CH2) bridge to a piperidine ring at its 4-position, giving a simple benzyl-substituted saturated heterocycle. The six-membered piperidine ring is fully saturated and adopts a chair-like conformation, while the aromatic phenyl ring is planar and unsubstituted, so the scaffold contains no ring fusion. The only heteroatom is the secondary amine nitrogen within the piperidine ring, which carries an N-H group that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The overall structure has a degree of rotational flexibility around the CH2 linker, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local mirror relationship of the piperidine ring.

This molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a three-carbon framework: a central quaternary carbon bearing a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, a carboxylic acid group, and a trifluoromethyl group. Because the central carbon is attached to four different substituents, it is a stereogenic center, so the molecule can exist as two mirror-image forms. There are no rings or ring fusions, and the structure is fairly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group and the hydroxyl group each supply hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the three fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group act only as weak acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is a thiobarbiturate-type ring: a six-membered pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione core in which one carbonyl oxygen at the 2-position is replaced by sulfur, giving a thiourea-like unit flanked by two amide carbonyls. The C5 carbon of this ring bears an exocyclic double bond linked to a 5-bromofuran ring, creating a conjugated, largely planar arylidene system. The bromine sits at the 5-position of the furan, adjacent to the oxygen heteroatom, and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis of note. Two N–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the three carbonyl oxygens, the thiocarbonyl sulfur, and the furan oxygen serve as acceptors. The extended conjugation keeps the scaffold fairly rigid.

This molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. The ring carries an ethyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is attached to an ethyl chain) on one carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, along with two hydroxyl groups and a methyl group at other positions around the ring. The hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, while the ester carbonyl oxygen, the ester ether oxygen, and the ring nitrogen can accept them. The ring is planar and rigid, while the ethyl ester tail adds some conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

text: This molecule is an acyclic tertiary amine built on a simple linear scaffold: a central nitrogen bearing one methyl group and two unbranched eight-carbon chains. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the single amine nitrogen. The two octyl arms are identical, so the molecule has approximate mirror symmetry through the nitrogen and the methyl group. Its long saturated chains give it considerable conformational flexibility with no rigid elements. The nitrogen lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a saturated five-membered carbocyclic ring (a cyclopentane) bearing three quaternary-type carbons: one ring carbon carries both a methyl group and a carboxylic acid, and an adjacent ring carbon carries two methyl groups, giving a gem-dimethyl arrangement. The third ring carbon bears a two-carbon ethyl linker terminating in an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the aromatic group is attached through a flexible chain rather than fused to the cycloalkane. The compound has no ring fusion and no internal symmetry, because the substituents are placed asymmetrically around the ring. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the aromatic ring and the saturated carbon framework contribute no additional hydrogen-bonding capability. Overall, the rigid cyclopentane core contrasts with the rotatable chain connecting the phenyl group.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. An ethoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to an ethyl chain) is attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a bromine atom sits on a carbon further around the ring, creating a 2,5-disubstitution pattern. The ring is planar and fully unsaturated, and the ethoxy chain adds some conformational flexibility, though the core remains rigid. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ether oxygen provides a second, weaker acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered pyrrole-type ring that contains an N-H group. The ring system is planar and rigid, with the fusion sharing a C-C bond between the two rings. An aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen) is attached to the carbon at position 3 of the five-membered ring, while a bromine atom sits on the benzene portion at position 5. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single minor axis of asymmetry from the substitution pattern. The indole N-H acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the aldehyde oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.
